questions.q: What is the exact amount of money Lencho receives in the envelope, and what amount did he originally request from God in his first letter?
questions.a: Lencho receives 70 pesos but requested 100 pesos in his first letter. A wrong answer (e.g., saying he received 100 pesos or requested 70) reveals the student has not read the text closely or is confusing the two letters — a common error where students mix up the request and the response amounts, leading to incorrect irony analysis.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Lencho becomes angry after counting the money, even though he asked God for help and received some money.
questions.a: Lencho becomes angry because he believes God would never make a mistake or send less than asked; therefore, the missing 30 pesos must have been stolen by the post office employees. A wrong answer (e.g., "he is greedy" or "he is ungrateful") reveals the student misses the crucial point: Lencho's anger stems from his *absolute faith in God's perfection*, not ingratitude — he genuinely thinks God sent 100 pesos and humans stole the rest.

questions.q: Apply the concept of situational irony to this scene: State the expectation (what the postmaster intends) and the reality (what Lencho believes), and explain why the gap between them creates irony.
questions.a: Expectation: The postmaster and employees collect 70 pesos out of kindness to help Lencho, hoping he will feel grateful. Reality: Lencho believes God sent the full 100 pesos and accuses the very same helpers of stealing 30 pesos. The irony: The helpers' generosity is repaid with suspicion. A wrong answer that only defines irony without applying it to these two specific perspectives shows the student cannot connect the literary term to textual evidence — a key board exam skill.

questions.q: Analyze how Lencho's second letter to God ("God: Of the money I asked for, only seventy pesos reached me. Send me the rest, since I need it very much. But don't send it to me through the mail because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.") reveals his character. What two opposing traits does it highlight?
questions.a: The letter highlights (1) unwavering faith in God — he writes to God again without doubt, and (2) deep distrust of humans — he calls the post office employees "crooks" despite their kindness. A wrong answer listing only one trait (e.g., only "faithful" or only "suspicious") reveals the student fails to see the *contrast* that defines Lencho's complexity and drives the story's irony.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Lencho's anger at receiving 70 pesos is justified because he needed 100 pesos to replant his fields." Defend or critique using textual evidence.
questions.a: Critique: While his need is real (hailstorm destroyed crops), his anger is *misplaced* — the text shows the postmaster "experienced the contentment of a man who has performed a good deed," and the employees gave "part of their salary." Lencho's anger ignores this human generosity. A wrong answer that agrees without qualification reveals the student cannot evaluate character motivation beyond surface-level need — a higher-order skill the board exam tests.

questions.q: Create a 3-4 sentence alternate ending where Lencho discovers the truth about the 70 pesos. Show how this would change the irony of the story.
questions.a: Example: "When the postmaster confesses, Lencho falls to his knees, realizing God worked *through* humans. He writes a third letter: 'God, thank you for giving me neighbours with hearts like yours.' The irony shifts from *situational* (helpers called crooks) to *dramatic* (reader knows truth before Lencho) and resolves in gratitude." A poor answer that just has Lencho say "thank you" without showing the *shift in understanding* reveals the student cannot manipulate irony types — a creative application skill.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Lencho's anger at receiving 70 pesos instead of the 100 he requested from God demonstrates ______ irony: the outcome is the opposite of what is expected — the postmaster and employees who generously collected money to help Lencho are accused by him of stealing the missing 30 pesos, revealing Lencho's absolute faith in God but complete distrust of human beings.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you helped a friend anonymously by collecting money from classmates, but when they receive it, they thank God and accuse your classmates of ______ part of it — how would you feel?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Identify the specific textual evidence showing Lencho's reaction to the 70 pesos, (2) Explain why this reaction constitutes situational irony by contrasting the postmaster's intention with Lencho's interpretation, and (3) Write a structured board-exam answer using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence.
